questions.q: A package worked perfectly for every app in its own monorepo, but users of the published version get TS7016. Why did the monorepo not show the problem?
questions.explain: A workspace link exposes the folder; the registry only receives the tarball. Test what users receive: npm pack --dry-run, publint, and an install of the .tgz file.
options: The monorepo used an older TypeScript version
Workspaces link the whole package folder, so the .d.ts files were on disk even though files kept them out of the tarball
npm strips declaration files from every published package

questions.q: Why does a TypeScript library publish compiled .js files instead of its .ts sources as the entry point?
questions.explain: Consumers run and check the compiled output. The source may still be published (for declaration maps), but it is never what exports points at.
options: Node.js will not strip types inside node_modules, bundlers expect JavaScript there, and users' compilers should not re-check your source with their settings
Declaration files can only describe .js files in the same folder

questions.q: Why does the lesson's tsconfig.build.json start with "extends": "./tsconfig.json"?
questions.explain: Two independent configs drift apart: code could pass npm run check with one set of rules and be built with another. Extending keeps one source of truth and overrides only the build-specific options.
options: TypeScript requires every config to extend another one
So the build uses exactly the same strictness and module settings as the check, and only adds what building needs (emit, rootDir, outDir, declarations, include/exclude)
So that the build also compiles the tests
So that noEmit stays on during the build

questions.q: With "rootDir": "src" and "outDir": "dist", where does src/money/format.ts compile to?
questions.explain: The folder structure inside rootDir is copied into outDir. Without rootDir: "src", the src folder itself would appear inside dist, and the exports paths would be wrong.

questions.q: You publish dist/index.d.ts.map but not src/. What happens when a user presses "go to definition" on one of your functions?
questions.explain: A declaration map is only useful together with the source it points to. Publish src (without tests) as well, or do not bother with declaration maps.
options: The editor opens your TypeScript source from GitHub
The map points at ../src/index.ts, which is not in the package, so the editor falls back to the .d.ts file
The editor shows an error and refuses to open anything

questions.q: Why must "types" come first inside an exports entry?
questions.explain: The first matching condition wins. TypeScript matches types plus the runtime conditions, so types must be ahead of them. Node.js ignores types entirely.
options: JSON objects are sorted alphabetically by npm
Node.js reads "types" to decide which JavaScript file to load
Conditions are checked in the order written, and TypeScript also matches "import", "require" and "default", so if one of those came first TypeScript would stop there
It is only a style convention

questions.q: An entry is written { "default": "./dist/index.js", "import": "./dist/index.mjs" }. Which file does an import load?
questions.explain: Node.js walks the conditions in order and takes the first match. default always matches, so everything after it is dead. Put default last.
options: ./dist/index.js, because default matches everything and comes first
Neither: Node.js reports an invalid exports map

questions.q: An ESM-only package maps "." to { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "import": "./dist/index.js" }. A CommonJS user on Node.js 24 writes require("@naija-shop/naira"). What happens?
questions.explain: Node.js can load ES modules with require, but only if the exports map offers a condition that require matches. "types" matches for TypeScript, so the compiler is happy. Using "default" for the JavaScript serves both.
options: It works, because Node.js 24 can require ES modules
Their type check passes, but Node.js throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED: no condition matches require
Their type check fails with TS7016

questions.q: A package's exports lists only ".". A user writes import { parseNaira } from "@naija-shop/naira/dist/index.js". What happens?
questions.explain: An exports map hides every path it does not list, in both tools. That is what lets you reorganise dist without a major release.
options: It works, because the file exists in node_modules
TypeScript reports "Cannot find module" (TS2307) and Node.js throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED
It works in Node.js but not in TypeScript
It works in TypeScript but not in Node.js

questions.q: A package has "files": ["dist", "src", "!src/**/*.test.ts"]. Which of these ends up in the tarball?
questions.explain: files is an allow-list, and ! removes matches again. npm always adds package.json, the README and the licence file. Everything else unlisted, secrets included, stays out.
options: package.json and README.md, even though they are not listed

questions.q: What is the difference between publint and attw?
questions.explain: They overlap a little but catch different mistakes. In the lesson, publint caught the unpublished .d.ts, while attw caught "masquerading as ESM" declarations in the dual package.
options: They do the same thing; attw is newer

publint checks that package.json fields, condition order and published files are consistent; attw resolves the package as different TypeScript settings would and compares the types found with the JavaScript that runs
publint checks types, attw checks JavaScript
publint publishes the package, attw tests it

questions.q: Run on the broken 1.0.0 package (no .d.ts in the tarball), attw printed "This package does not contain types." What was its exit code, and what follows for CI?
questions.explain: A tool's exit code is what CI acts on. Know how each check reports failure, and combine checks: publint's errors fail the job.
options: 1, so CI would have stopped the release
0, so attw alone would not have stopped the release; publint, which exited non-zero, would

questions.q: attw reports "Masquerading as ESM" for CommonJS consumers of a dual package. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Each condition needs matching declarations: "import": { "types": esm .d.ts, "default": esm .js } and "require": { "types": cjs .d.ts, "default": cjs .js }, with cjs/package.json saying "type": "commonjs".
options: CommonJS consumers are given the ESM declaration files (for example through one shared top-level "types"), so their types describe a module format they do not get
The package has no ESM build

questions.q: What causes the dual-package hazard?
questions.explain: Two builds are two modules. An error made by one copy is not an instance of the other copy's class, and state kept in one is invisible to the other. The identical declarations hide it from the compiler.
options: One application loading both the ESM and the CommonJS build, which creates two separate copies of every class, cache and piece of module state

questions.q: Which is the most reliable way to avoid the dual-package hazard for a new library that targets Node.js 24?
questions.explain: One build means one copy. CommonJS-only would also avoid the hazard but gives up ES module benefits; on Node.js 24 there is no reason to. If two copies are unavoidable, check errors by name, code or a Symbol.for brand.
options: Ship ESM only, with a "default" condition, so import and require load the same single copy
Give the two builds different class names

questions.q: Two copies of the same error class stand in for the ESM and CommonJS builds of a dual package. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call creates a new class, just as each build creates its own. instanceof only recognises instances of the exact class object; the name and code properties travel with the error and work across copies.

questions.q: Two module copies each create a brand symbol. What does this print?
questions.explain: Symbol() makes a new, unique symbol every time. Symbol.for(key) looks the key up in a global registry shared by the whole program, so both copies get the same symbol. That is why a Symbol.for brand survives the dual-package hazard.

questions.q: The lesson's defence checks error.name. What does this print?
questions.explain: A subclass inherits name from Error.prototype, which is "Error", unless it sets its own. Checking by name only works if the library sets it, as PaymentError does.

questions.q: This function follows an exports entry the way Node.js and TypeScript do: the first condition that matches wins. What does it print?
questions.explain: default matches everything and comes first, so TypeScript (conditions types and import) gets the JavaScript file instead of the declarations. publint reports exactly this.

questions.q: Using the same resolve function, what does this print for a dual package?
questions.explain: TypeScript resolving a require uses types and require, and reaches the CommonJS declarations. Node.js importing gets the ESM JavaScript. With neither import nor require in the list, nothing matches, because this entry has no top-level default.

questions.q: Your published dist/index.d.ts contains import type { Logger } from "@zudojs/logger". Where must @zudojs/logger be listed?
questions.explain: Your declarations are compiled by your users. A package they mention must be installed for them, which only happens for dependencies and peerDependencies.
options: devDependencies, because it is only used for types
dependencies (or peerDependencies), because every user's compiler must find it to read your declarations
Nowhere; TypeScript ignores types from other packages in .d.ts files

questions.q: Version 1.1.0 adds a required locale property to the exported FormatOptions interface. The JavaScript still works without it. What kind of change is this?
questions.explain: For a TypeScript package, "breaking" includes "no longer compiles". Make the new property optional with a default and it becomes a minor release.
options: Major: users who build a FormatOptions object without locale no longer compile
None: types are not covered by semver

questions.q: Which change to a published function's types is breaking for its callers?
questions.explain: A wider return type forces every caller to handle the new case, so existing code stops compiling (or, worse, crashes if it used an assertion). Wider parameters and new overloads keep old calls valid.
options: Adding an optional parameter at the end

questions.q: A package adds a required currency property to an interface it returns (Receipt). Callers who only read receipts are fine. Who can still break?
questions.explain: Output types are also input types for anyone who implements or fakes them. Their object literals now lack currency. Think in both directions when an exported interface changes.
options: Users who create their own Receipt objects, such as fakes in tests or implementations of an interface that returns one

questions.q: Version 2 of a parser widened its return type to include undefined, but a caller written for version 1 used a non-null assertion. What does this print?
questions.explain: The ! silenced the compiler, so the new undefined case reached toFixed and threw. Callers who checked === null honestly would have got a compile error instead: that is why a wider return type is a major change.

questions.q: A release script sorts published versions as strings. What does this print?
questions.explain: String sorting compares character by character, and "9" is greater than "1", so 1.9.0 looks newest. Versions must be compared part by part as numbers (and real semver also handles prereleases), which is why tools use a semver library.

questions.q: In a .cts file, why does the lesson prefer const naira: typeof import("@naija-shop/naira") = require("@naija-shop/naira") over import naira = require("@naija-shop/naira")?
questions.explain: Node.js type stripping only removes types; it cannot rewrite import =. Erasable syntax keeps every runner (tsc, tsx, Node.js) working on the same file.
options: The import … = require form does not type-check
Both type-check, but import … = require is not erasable syntax, so node legacy.cts refuses it; the require call is plain JavaScript plus a type

questions.q: In TypeScript 7, which settings produce a CommonJS build of an ESM library in the lesson?
questions.explain: node10 resolution was removed (error TS5108), and NodeNext resolution requires module: NodeNext. With verbatimModuleSyntax on, export in a file emitted as CommonJS is error TS1287.
options: "module": "NodeNext" alone, because it emits both formats
A .cjs extension on every source file

questions.q: You add "./parse": "./dist/parse.js" to exports (a plain string, no conditions), and dist/parse.d.ts is published next to it. Does import { parseNaira } from "@naija-shop/naira/parse" get types?
questions.explain: After resolving the JavaScript file, TypeScript looks for a declaration with the same name beside it. Relying on that works until someone moves the declarations into a separate folder; explicit conditions say what you mean.
options: No, a subpath without a "types" condition is always untyped
Yes, TypeScript finds the sibling parse.d.ts next to the resolved .js file, but an explicit { "types", "default" } pair is clearer and does not depend on file placement
Only if parse.d.ts is listed in files separately

questions.q: A package keeps an exchange-rate cache in module state. Here two calls stand in for the ESM and CommonJS builds being loaded by one application. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each copy has its own cache. Code that went through the CommonJS build never sees the rate the ESM build stored. The dual-package hazard is not only about instanceof; every piece of module state is doubled.

questions.q: A declaration map inside an installed package says "sources": ["../src/index.ts"]. Paths in a map are relative to the map file. Where will the editor look for the source?
questions.explain: The path is resolved against the map's own folder (dist/), so ../src/index.ts is inside the package. If src is not in files, that file does not exist and "go to definition" falls back to the .d.ts.

questions.q: Condition order in package.json matters because the parsed object keeps it. What does this print?
questions.explain: String keys keep the order in which they were written, so what you type in package.json is exactly the order Node.js and TypeScript check. Nothing sorts them for you.
options:
default then types
types not first

types then default
types not first

questions.q: A subpath in exports can be a plain string. Using the lesson's resolve rules (first matching condition wins, strings match directly), what does this print?
questions.explain: For "./parse" TypeScript resolves the JavaScript file and then has to find parse.d.ts beside it on its own. A deep path that is not a key is simply not exported. Giving each subpath its own types/default pair removes the guesswork.

questions.q: Write resolve(entry, conditions): given an exports entry (a path string, or an object of conditions whose values are entries) and the list of active conditions, walk the object keys in order and return the path of the first matching condition, recursing into nested objects. "default" always matches. Return null when nothing matches.
questions.explain: Order is everything: TypeScript's first match is types; Node.js with require skips types and enters node; a browser bundler matches neither and falls through to default. If a nested object matches nothing, the walk continues with the next key.

questions.q: Write lintEntry(entry) in the spirit of publint: for a conditions object, return a list of problems: "types must be first" if a types key exists but is not the first key, and "default must be last" if a default key exists but is not the last. Print the problems for each entry, or ok.
questions.explain: JavaScript objects keep string keys in insertion order, which is also the order they were written in the JSON, so Object.keys shows the order Node.js and TypeScript will check.
questions.expected:
ok
types must be first; default must be last
types must be first

questions.q: Given the list of files in a tarball and a package's exports (subpath to { types, default }), print one line per target that is not in the tarball, in the form <subpath> <condition> <path> is not published, or all targets published. Paths in exports start with ./; tarball paths do not.
questions.explain: This is publint's third error from the lesson: the exports map promises a file that files kept out of the tarball. Comparing against the tarball list, not the folder, is the whole point.

questions.q: Write releaseFor(changes): given a list of changes to a package's public types, return "major" if any change is breaking, otherwise "minor" if any adds something, otherwise "patch". Breaking: "remove-export", "required-input-property", "wider-return", "narrower-parameter". Adding: "new-export", "optional-input-property", "wider-parameter". Anything else is a patch.
questions.explain: A release is as big as its biggest change. One wider return type makes the whole release major, however many harmless additions come with it.

questions.q: Make isPaymentError work across two copies of the payments module. Mark every PaymentError with a brand property keyed by Symbol.for("@naija-shop/payment-error"), and check for that brand instead of using instanceof.
questions.explain: Symbol.for returns the same symbol in every copy, so the brand set by one copy is recognised by the other. (The solution also replaces the parameter property with a plain field, which keeps the code erasable.)

questions.q: Write nextVersion(version, release) for plain major.minor.patch versions: a major bump resets minor and patch to 0, a minor bump resets patch to 0.
questions.explain: Each part is a number, so 1.9.0 plus a minor release is 1.10.0, not 2.0.0. This is what npm version patch|minor|major does to package.json.

questions.q: The package says "engines": { "node": ">=24" }. Write supports(required, running) for requirements of the form ">=N" (N a major version) and running versions like "v24.19.0" or "22.12.0".
questions.explain: npm only warns when engines does not match, so a package or server that truly needs Node.js 24 (for example for require of ES modules) should also check at startup, comparing the major version as a number.
